findings.claim: The reader identifies a media rule with startsWith("@media") and the query extractor permits zero whitespace after @media. Replacing both solved @media rules with the invalid unknown at-rule @mediascreen and (...) therefore still produces pass 7/fail 0, while Chromium at 700px keeps one card column and at 1100px keeps .page display:block. Public success can still be reported when tasks 4 and 5 do not work in the browser.

evidence.section: 4.3.1 Consume a token and 5.4.2 Parse a stylesheet: an at-keyword token starts one at-rule whose name is its ident sequence; @mediascreen is not @media
3 Syntax: media-query-list and media-query grammar for the @media rule

findings.recommendation: Recognize the @media at-rule token exactly (ASCII case-insensitively) rather than by prefix, require a real token boundary, and add a negative public regression for @mediascreen that also confirms the 700px and 1100px browser outcomes do not falsely pass.

findings.claim: Two semantically exact mobile-first spellings remain false failures. CSS media-query tokens are ASCII case-insensitive, but solved @MEDIA rules fail tasks 4, 5, and the mobile-first check. The exact breakpoints (min-width: 600.0px) and (min-width: 1000.0px) apply at 600px and 1000px in Chromium, but fail the same three public checks because equality and the ordering regex accept only canonical integer text.

evidence.section: 3 Syntax (tokens are ASCII case-insensitive) and 2.4.3 range context for equivalent width comparisons
5.3 Real Numbers and 5.4 Numbers with Units: dimensions can use numbers with fractional components

findings.recommendation: Parse the @media name ASCII case-insensitively and compare px dimensions numerically before matching the exact 600px and 1000px outcomes. Add passing regressions for @MEDIA and decimal-equivalent px breakpoints while retaining rejection of non-px, strict-boundary, wrong-direction, compound, print, and malformed conditions.

findings.claim: A valid solved layout that defines --one-column: 1fr and --two-columns: repeat(2, 1fr), then uses var(--one-column) and var(--two-columns) for .cards, renders one column below 600px and two from 600px in Chromium but fails public task 4. The reader compares unresolved source text rather than the computed value. Its blanket comma normalization also changes a custom-property string value such as --label: "a,b" to "a, b", so cleanValue is not a semantics-preserving custom-property token normalizer.

evidence.section: 2 Defining Custom Properties and 3 Using Cascading Variables: var() substitutes the computed custom-property value into another property

findings.recommendation: Evaluate the relevant computed grid value in the existing pinned browser, or resolve custom-property substitution with a conforming CSS parser before comparison. Keep normalization token-aware so commas and parenthesis-like text inside strings are not rewritten. Add a passing custom-property-indirection route and a unit test that preserves quoted custom-property tokens.
